endocapillary_hypercellularity: Increased Cellular Density within Glomerular Capillaries
Look for an increased number of cells within the capillary lumina, making the capillary loops appear more crowded and less open than normal.

Identify the presence of various inflammatory cells, such as neutrophils, macrophages, and lymphocytes, within the capillary loops. This is indicative of an inflammatory process contributing to hypercellularity.

Observe the mesangial areas for an increased number of mesangial cells and matrix. While this primarily contributes to mesangial hypercellularity, it can often be associated with endocapillary hypercellularity.
Check for the narrowing or occlusion of capillary lumens due to the increased cellular content. This can lead to reduced capillary lumina visibility.
Determine whether the hypercellularity is segmental (affecting parts of the glomerulus) or global (affecting the entire glomerulus). Endocapillary hypercellularity can be either.
Look for signs of endothelial cell swelling, which can contribute to the overall hypercellular appearance of the capillary loops.
Assess the glomerular basement membrane for any signs of thickening or disruption, although these changes are secondary and not always present.
In some staining techniques, particularly with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E), areas of endocapillary hypercellularity might appear more eosinophilic due to the increased cellular content.
exudative_glomerulus: Look for the presence of eosinophilic (pink-staining) material within the capillary lumina, which represents hyaline thrombi. These are composed of plasma proteins that have leaked out of the bloodstream and aggregated within the glomerulus.

Identify fibrin deposits within the glomerular capillaries, which can appear as irregular, fibrillar, or amorphous eosinophilic material. Fibrin deposition is indicative of ongoing inflammation and coagulation.

Observe thickened capillary walls, often due to the accumulation of immune complexes and other plasma proteins. This thickening can sometimes make the capillary loops appear more prominent and less distinct.
Assess for any signs of disruption or irregularities in the glomerular basement membrane, which can be due to the deposition of immune complexes and the exudative process.

Identify the presence of neutrophils within the glomerular capillaries and in the mesangial areas. Neutrophilic infiltration is a hallmark of acute inflammation and can contribute to the exudative appearance.
Look for lipid droplets within the glomerular tuft, which can be seen in some cases of exudative glomerulopathy. These appear as clear vacuoles within cells and are often found in macrophages.

Recognize areas of mesangiolysis, where the mesangial matrix is dissolved or disrupted. This can lead to areas of clearing within the mesangium, often associated with the presence of inflammatory cells and exudative material

Evaluate the overall cellularity of the glomerulus. While not as pronounced as in endocapillary hypercellularity, there can be an increase in cells due to the inflammatory infiltrate and exudative process
In periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) staining, look for PAS-positive material within the glomerulus. This can highlight areas of hyaline deposits and other exudative material
fibrinoid_necrosis_glomerulus: Fibrinoid Material

Look for areas within the glomerulus that contain fibrinoid material. This appears as intensely eosinophilic (pink-staining) amorphous or fibrillar material within the glomerular tuft, often seen with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining.
Disruption of Glomerular Architecture

Identify regions where the normal glomerular architecture is disrupted. This includes the breakdown of the glomerular basement membrane and the capillary walls, leading to a more chaotic and disorganized appearance.
Cell Necrosis

Observe the presence of necrotic cells within the glomerulus. Necrotic cells may appear as ghost cells or cells with pyknotic nuclei (condensed, dark-staining nuclei) and karyorrhexis (fragmented nuclei).
Inflammatory Cell Infiltration
Note the infiltration of inflammatory cells, particularly neutrophils, within the areas of necrosis. The presence of these cells is indicative of an acute inflammatory response
Fibrin Deposits
Look for deposits of fibrin within the glomerulus. These may be found within the necrotic areas and appear as bright red strands in fibrin-stained sections.
Capillary Wall Rupture
Identify ruptures or breaks in the glomerular capillary walls. This can lead to the leakage of blood components into the glomerular tuft, contributing to the fibrinoid appearance
Extravasation of Red Blood Cells
Check for the presence of extravasated red blood cells within the glomerulus, often seen in association with capillary wall rupture and necrosis
Hyaline Thrombi
Note any hyaline thrombi within the capillary lumina. These are composed of plasma proteins and can contribute to the overall fibrinoid necrosis appearance
Glomerular Basement Membrane (GBM) Changes
Assess for irregularities or disruption of the GBM. In areas of fibrinoid necrosis, the GBM may appear fragmented or discontinuous
Vascular Changes

Look for similar necrotic changes in the vessels adjacent to or within the glomerulus. This can include fibrinoid necrosis of arterioles or small arteries, which often accompanies severe glomerular injury
fibrocellular_crescent: Look for crescent-shaped cellular proliferations located between the glomerular basement membrane (GBM) and Bowman's capsule. These crescents typically encircle part of the glomerular tuft.

Identify the presence of both inflammatory cells (such as macrophages, lymphocytes, and occasionally neutrophils) and proliferating parietal epithelial cells within the crescent. This mixed cellularity is a hallmark of fibrocellular crescents.
Observe for the presence of newly formed fibrous tissue within the crescent. This fibrous tissue may appear as pink, fibrillar material with H&E staining and indicates early stages of fibrosis.
Note the compression or collapse of the glomerular tuft due to the expansion of the crescent. This can lead to a reduction in the size of the capillary loops within the tuft

Look for the deposition of extracellular matrix components within the crescent, contributing to its fibrous appearance. This deposition can be highlighted with special stains such as Masson's trichrome, which stains collagen blue
Determine whether the crescent formation is segmental (affecting a portion of the glomerulus) or global (involving the entire circumference of the glomerulus). Fibrocellular crescents can be either.
Assess the proliferation of parietal epithelial cells lining Bowman's capsule. These cells are actively proliferating and contributing to the crescent formation

Identify the presence of fibrin and other proteinaceous material within the crescent. These deposits can be seen as bright red with fibrin stains like Martius scarlet blue (MSB) or by immunofluorescence for fibrin
Check for associated interstitial inflammation and tubulitis in the areas surrounding the affected glomerulus. This can indicate an ongoing inflammatory process contributing to the crescent formation
fibrous_crescent: Look for dense, collagen-rich fibrous tissue within the crescent. This tissue often stains blue with Masson's trichrome stain and appears eosinophilic (pink) with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining

Identify the absence or very sparse presence of cellular elements such as inflammatory cells or proliferating epithelial cells within the crescent. Unlike fibrocellular crescents, fibrous crescents are mainly composed of acellular fibrous tissue
Observe the crescentic (semi-lunar) shape of the fibrous tissue located between Bowman's capsule and the glomerular tuft. This shape partially or completely surrounds the glomerular tuft
Note the compression or collapse of the glomerular tuft due to the expansive fibrous crescent. This can lead to a reduction in the visibility of capillary loops within the tuft
Look for adhesion of the fibrous tissue to Bowman's capsule, which can be prominent in chronic lesions
Determine whether the fibrous crescent formation is segmental (involving a portion of the glomerulus) or global (encircling the entire glomerulus). Fibrous crescents can display either pattern
Check for evidence of glomerulosclerosis, where parts or all of the glomerular tuft may be replaced by sclerotic tissue. This is often seen in conjunction with fibrous crescents
Assess the surrounding renal parenchyma for signs of interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy, which often accompany chronic glomerular lesions and are indicative of long-standing damage
Look for thickening and sclerosis of Bowman's capsule itself, which can occur as part of the chronic fibrotic process
glomerul_lipoprotein_thrombus: Look for hyaline thrombi, which appear as eosinophilic (pink-staining) and homogeneous material within the capillary lumina on hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining.
Identify the presence of lipid within the thrombi. This can be confirmed using special stains for lipids, such as Oil Red O or Sudan IV, which stain lipids red or orange, respectively
Look for foamy macrophages within or near the thrombi. These macrophages contain lipid vacuoles, giving them a foamy appearance
Observe for distension or expansion of the glomerular capillary loops due to the presence of thrombi. This can cause the loops to appear dilated and filled with the hyaline material
Note that the thrombi are located within the glomerular capillaries, leading to partial or complete occlusion of the capillary lumina
Using PAS staining, the thrombi may appear magenta, highlighting the presence of lipoprotein and other carbohydrate-rich substances within the thrombi
Unlike inflammatory thrombi, lipoprotein thrombi typically have minimal associated inflammatory cell infiltration within the glomerular tuft

Check for concurrent vascular changes in the renal arterioles, such as arteriosclerosis or hyaline arteriosclerosis, which might be associated with conditions that lead to lipoprotein thrombus formation
glomerular_adhesion: Segmental Attachment
Look for areas where the glomerular tuft is attached to Bowman's capsule. This can be focal, involving only a segment of the glomerular circumference
Disruption of Bowman's Space

Note the disruption or obliteration of Bowman's space in areas where the adhesion occurs. Normally, Bowman's space should be a clear, crescent-shaped area between the glomerular tuft and Bowman's capsule
Sclerosis at the Adhesion Site

Identify any sclerosis (hyalinization or scarring) at the site of adhesion. This can appear as increased extracellular matrix or collagen deposition, often highlighted with special stains like Masson's trichrome (which stains collagen blue).
Crescent Formation

In some cases, adhesions may be associated with crescent formation. Crescents are composed of proliferating epithelial cells and inflammatory cells that occupy Bowman's space and may adhere to the glomerular tuft
Capillary Loop Disruption
Observe any disruption or distortion of the normal capillary loop architecture in the area of adhesion. This can be due to the fibrotic process pulling the capillaries towards Bowman's capsule
Inflammatory Cells
Look for the presence of inflammatory cells (such as macrophages, lymphocytes) around the adhesion site, which can indicate an ongoing inflammatory process contributing to the adhesion.
Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS) Stain
Using PAS staining, the areas of adhesion might show increased staining due to the presence of more extracellular matrix material.
Proliferating Parietal Epithelial Cells
Note any proliferation of parietal epithelial cells lining Bowman's capsule, which can contribute to the formation of adhesions.
Bowman's Capsule Thickening
Check for thickening of Bowman's capsule at the site of adhesion. This thickening can be due to fibrosis or the accumulation of extracellular matrix
Overall Glomerular Architecture
Assess the overall architecture of the glomerulus. Adhesions can lead to segmental or global distortion of the glomerular structure, depending on their extent and severity
glomerular_basement_membrane_duplication: Look for double contours of the GBM, which appear as two parallel lines surrounding the capillary loops when viewed under light microscopy. These double contours are best visualized with silver stains (e.g., Jones' methenamine silver) or periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stain.
Identify the 'tram-track' appearance, where the duplicated GBM resembles railroad tracks. This is a hallmark of GBM duplication and is most prominently seen in silver-stained sections
Although not visible under light microscopy, electron microscopy would reveal electron-dense deposits within the lamina rara interna or lamina densa, which contribute to the splitting of the GBM

Observe the presence of subendothelial immune deposits, which can be highlighted with immunofluorescence microscopy, showing granular or linear staining patterns depending on the underlying cause (e.g., immune complex deposition)

Look for evidence of mesangial interposition, where mesangial cells and matrix extend into the peripheral capillary loops and contribute to the appearance of GBM splitting. This can be seen in light microscopy but is better appreciated with electron microscopy
Note any thickening of the GBM, which can accompany duplication. Thickening can be irregular and associated with the double contour appearance
Assess the capillary walls for irregularities, such as segmental areas of GBM duplication alternating with normal GBM segments.
Look for proliferation of endothelial and mesangial cells, which can be associated with the process of GBM splitting.
Using specific stains like PAS or Jones' methenamine silver, the duplicated GBM will stain more prominently, making it easier to differentiate the two layers.
glomerular_basement_membrane_thickening: Increased Thickness of the GBM
Look for an overall increase in the thickness of the GBM surrounding the glomerular capillaries. This can be best appreciated with appropriate staining techniques
Staining Techniques

Utilize specific stains that highlight the GBM. Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stain makes the GBM appear magenta, while silver stains (e.g., Jones' methenamine silver) make it appear black. Thickening will result in a more prominent and wider appearance of the GBM with these stains
Homogeneous Appearance
Observe the GBM for a homogeneous, thickened appearance. In uniformly thickened GBM, the increased width will be consistent around the capillary loops
Lamellation

In electron microscopy, look for lamellation or 'splitting' of the GBM into multiple layers, which can sometimes accompany thickening. This finding is more specific and can be observed at a higher magnification
Irregular Thickening
Assess for irregular or segmental thickening of the GBM, which may be more pronounced in certain glomerular diseases. Some regions of the GBM may appear thicker than others
Capillary Loop Contours
Note the contours of the capillary loops, which may appear more rigid or less flexible due to the thickened GBM
Immune Deposits

Identify the presence of immune deposits that might cause or accompany thickening. These can be visualized with immunofluorescence microscopy showing granular or linear staining patterns for immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA) and complement (C3)
Basement Membrane Duplication
Differentiate from GBM duplication (splitting), where the appearance of double contours (tram-tracks) is observed, typically seen in membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN)
Associated Pathologies

Consider the context of underlying diseases commonly associated with GBM thickening, such as diabetic nephropathy, where thickening is diffuse and often accompanied by nodular glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules), or membranous nephropathy, where thickening is associated with subepithelial immune deposits
Comparative Normal GBM
Compare the thickness of the GBM to the normal GBM in unaffected areas or glomeruli, if present, to appreciate the relative thickening
glomerular_collapse: Look for a marked reduction or obliteration of the capillary lumina. The capillary loops appear wrinkled, compressed, or shrunken
Determine if the collapse is segmental (affecting part of the glomerulus) or global (affecting the entire glomerulus)

Observe for an increase in the extracellular matrix, which can contribute to the collapsed appearance. This might be evident as increased staining with periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) or other matrix stains
Look for hypertrophy and hyperplasia of podocytes, which are the epithelial cells lining the outer surface of the glomerular capillaries. Podocytes may appear enlarged and proliferative
Identify any adhesions of the collapsed capillary loops to Bowman's capsule, which can be a feature of glomerular collapse
Note the retraction of the glomerular tuft towards the vascular pole, resulting in a reduced capillary surface area and diminished overall size of the glomerulus
Wrinkling of the Glomerular Basement Membrane (GBM)
Assess for wrinkling or folding of the GBM, which occurs due to the collapse of the capillary loops. This can be highlighted using PAS or silver stains
Look for accompanying interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy in the surrounding renal tissue, which often accompanies glomerular collapse and indicates chronic damage
Recognize a decrease in the overall cellularity of the glomerulus, particularly the endothelial and mesangial cells
glomerular_congestion: Look for capillary loops that appear enlarged or swollen due to the accumulation of excess blood. The lumina are more prominent compared to normal glomeruli
Observe an increased number of red blood cells (erythrocytes) within the capillary loops. The capillaries appear packed or filled with erythrocytes
Note the overall appearance of hyperemia, where the glomerulus looks more intensely red or congested in H&E-stained sections due to the high volume of blood
Identify any changes in the endothelial cells lining the capillaries, which may appear flattened or stretched due to the increased blood volume
Assess for expansion or distension of the capillary loops. This can make the glomerular tuft appear more open or less compact
Differentiate congestion from inflammatory processes by noting the absence of a significant number of inflammatory cells (such as neutrophils or lymphocytes) within the glomerular tuft
Ensure there is no significant thickening of the glomerular basement membrane (GBM), which can help differentiate congestion from chronic glomerular diseases
Examine the surrounding renal cortex for signs of congestion in the peritubular capillaries, which can often accompany glomerular congestion
glomerular_foam_cell: Look for cells within the glomerulus that appear foamy or vacuolated due to the accumulation of lipid droplets. These droplets can vary in size and distribution within the cytoplasm of the cells
Identify cells that appear larger than surrounding cells due to the presence of intracytoplasmic lipid vacuoles. Foam cells often have an enlarged and swollen appearance
Observe the cytoplasm of the cells, which may appear clear or pale due to the displacement of cellular organelles by lipid droplets
Note the presence of a centrally located nucleus within the foamy cells. The nucleus may appear pushed to the periphery by the accumulation of lipid droplets
Identify the location of foam cells within the glomerulus. They may be found within the capillary lumina, mesangium, or along the glomerular tuft
Look for signs of inflammation, such as the presence of other inflammatory cells like neutrophils or lymphocytes, which may accompany foam cell accumulation

Using staining techniques such as hematoxylin and eosin (H&E), foam cells may appear eosinophilic with foamy cytoplasm. Oil Red O or Sudan stains can specifically highlight lipid droplets within the cells

Consider underlying conditions associated with foam cell accumulation in the glomerulus, such as lipid nephrosis (lipoid nephrosis) in nephrotic syndrome, or in conditions like atheroembolic disease affecting renal vessels.
Evaluate the surrounding glomerular structures for context. Foam cells may be associated with changes in the glomerular basement membrane, mesangial proliferation, or other glomerular lesions
glomerular_hyaline_pseudothrombus: Look for a homogeneous, eosinophilic (pink-staining) material within the glomerular capillary lumina. This material appears smooth and lacks the fibrin strands seen in true thrombi
Identify the presence of hyaline material within the capillary lumina. Hyaline is an amorphous, acellular substance composed of proteins, glycoproteins, and other extracellular matrix components

Observe the uniform distribution of the hyaline material throughout the capillary loops. Unlike true thrombi, which may be irregularly shaped and variably distributed, hyaline pseudothrombi are typically evenly dispersed
Note the absence of vascular occlusion or obstruction of the capillary lumina by the hyaline material. Pseudothrombi do not impede blood flow and do not cause ischemic injury to the glomerulus
Differentiate hyaline pseudothrombi from true thrombi by the absence of endothelial cells within the material. Pseudothrombi consist primarily of acellular hyaline material

Look for the presence of inflammatory cells, such as macrophages or lymphocytes, surrounding the hyaline pseudothrombi. Inflammatory cells may be present as part of the response to glomerular injury or as a consequence of the pseudothrombus formation

Using staining techniques such as periodic acid-Schiff (PAS), the hyaline material stains positive, appearing magenta. However, unlike true thrombi, pseudothrombi lack the intricate fibrin network seen with fibrin stains
Recognize that hyaline pseudothrombi are often associated with various forms of glomerular injury, including glomerulosclerosis, diabetic nephropathy, and hypertensive nephrosclerosis
glomerular_hyalinosis: Look for the presence of homogeneous, eosinophilic (pink-staining) material within the glomerular tuft. This material typically fills the mesangial areas and may extend into the capillary loops
Identify the acellular nature of the hyaline material, lacking cellular components such as nuclei or cytoplasm. This distinguishes hyalinosis from cellular lesions
Observe the expansion of the mesangial matrix due to the deposition of hyaline material. This can lead to widening of the mesangial spaces and compression of the capillary loops
Note the globular appearance of the hyaline deposits, which may form discrete, rounded structures within the glomerulus. These globules can vary in size and distribution
Determine whether the hyalinosis is segmental (affecting part of the glomerulus) or global (involving the entire glomerulus). Segmental involvement may be indicative of localized injury or disease
Consider the presence of underlying conditions associated with glomerular hyalinosis, such as diabetes mellitus, hypertension, aging-related changes, or chronic kidney diseases
Differentiate hyalinosis from inflammatory lesions by the absence of inflammatory cell infiltration within the hyaline material. Hyalinosis is primarily composed of acellular matrix

Using staining techniques such as periodic acid-Schiff (PAS), the hyaline material stains positive, appearing magenta. However, unlike basement membrane material, hyaline material is typically located within the mesangium
Recognize that glomerular hyalinosis is often a progressive lesion associated with chronic glomerular injury and may contribute to glomerulosclerosis over time
glomerular_obsolesce: Identify glomeruli that appear shrunken, hyalinized, and devoid of normal glomerular structures. These glomeruli may appear smaller compared to adjacent normal glomeruli
Determine whether the obsolescent changes affect the entire glomerulus (global obsolescence) or only part of it (segmental obsolescence). Segmental involvement may suggest localized injury or disease

Note the absence or severe reduction in the number of patent capillary loops within the glomerular tuft. This reflects loss of functional capillary beds, contributing to reduced renal filtration capacity

Observe the presence of sclerotic changes within the glomerulus, including glomerular basement membrane thickening, mesangial expansion, and matrix deposition. These changes contribute to the loss of glomerular function
Glomerular obsolescence may present with a collapsing appearance, where the glomerular tuft appears compressed and wrinkled due to fibrotic changes and loss of cellular elements
Look for adhesions of the glomerular tuft to Bowman's capsule and interstitial fibrosis surrounding the obsolescent glomerulus. These findings indicate chronic and irreversible glomerular injury
Identify the presence of hyaline material within the sclerosed glomerulus, which appears homogeneously eosinophilic and acellular. This material may replace normal glomerular structures

Assess the surrounding renal parenchyma for signs of chronic kidney disease, such as interstitial fibrosis, tubular atrophy, and arteriosclerosis. These changes often accompany glomerular obsolescence
Differentiate obsolescent glomeruli from active inflammatory lesions by the absence of inflammatory cell infiltration and evidence of ongoing inflammation within the glomerulus
glomerular_segmental_sclerosis: Identify focal areas within the glomerulus where sclerosis and obliteration of capillary loops are present, affecting only a segment of the glomerular tuft
Observe areas within the glomerulus where the capillary loops are replaced by sclerotic material. This material appears eosinophilic and acellular
Look for adhesions between the sclerotic segment and Bowman's capsule, indicating the involvement of the glomerular pole in segmental sclerosis
Note the collapse or compression of the capillary loops within the sclerotic segment, which may appear shrunken and distorted compared to the surrounding normal capillary loops
Identify areas of hyalinosis within the sclerotic segment, where the mesangial matrix becomes homogenized and eosinophilic
Look for evidence of cellular proliferation, including mesangial cell proliferation and/or hypertrophy of parietal epithelial cells, which may accompany segmental sclerosis

Using stains like periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) or Masson's trichrome, observe segmental areas that stain differently from the surrounding normal glomerular tissue. Segmental sclerosis may appear more intensely stained
Differentiate segmental sclerosis from global sclerosis by the focal nature of the lesion. In global sclerosis, the entire glomerulus is affected uniformly
Look for adherent macrophages within the sclerotic segment, which may be phagocytosing debris or lipid material
glomerular_thrombus: Identify the presence of material within the glomerular capillary lumina, which appears as an eosinophilic (pink-staining) mass occupying the capillary loops
Look for delicate fibrin strands within the intraluminal material, which are characteristic of thrombi. Fibrin strands may be seen extending across the capillary lumina
Observe the degree of luminal occlusion caused by the thrombus. Thrombi can partially or completely obstruct the capillary lumina, leading to compromised blood flow within the glomerulus
Note the presence of aggregated erythrocytes within the thrombus, contributing to its reddish appearance. Erythrocytes may appear trapped within the fibrin network

Look for adherence of the thrombus to the glomerular endothelium, particularly along the inner aspect of the capillary loops. This adherence may contribute to the stability and persistence of the thrombus
Observe distortion or compression of the capillary loops surrounding the thrombus, which may appear flattened or compressed due to the luminal obstruction
Identify signs of associated inflammation, such as infiltrating leukocytes (e.g., neutrophils), which may be present in the vicinity of the thrombus as part of the host response to vascular injury

Consider the presence of underlying endothelial injury or dysfunction, which may predispose to thrombus formation. Endothelial injury can be identified by changes such as endothelial cell swelling or detachment

Using staining techniques such as periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) or silver stains, observe the thrombus for characteristic staining patterns, which may help differentiate it from other intraluminal materials
glomerulomegaly: Identify glomeruli that appear larger than adjacent normal glomeruli or larger than expected for the age and size of the kidney
Observe the expansion of the glomerular tuft, which may protrude into Bowman's space and occupy a larger area of the renal cortex
Look for dilatation or engorgement of the glomerular capillary loops within the enlarged glomerulus. The capillary loops may appear distended and filled with blood
Note the increased density of nuclei within the enlarged glomerulus, reflecting hypercellularity. This may be indicative of cellular proliferation or hypertrophy
Identify expansion of the mesangial matrix within the glomerulus, contributing to the enlargement of the glomerular tuft
Assess for thickening of the GBM surrounding the capillary loops. Glomerulomegaly may be associated with GBM thickening, although this is not always present
Look for evidence of mesangial cell proliferation within the enlarged glomerulus. Mesangial cells may appear hypertrophic or hyperplastic
Observe distortion or alteration in the configuration of the glomerular capillary loops within the enlarged glomerulus. The capillary loops may appear irregular or tortuous
Identify hypertrophied podocytes along the glomerular tuft, which may contribute to the enlargement of the glomerulus. Hypertrophied podocytes may appear enlarged and contain prominent nuclei
glomerulonephritis_hyaline_thrombus: Identify the presence of homogeneously eosinophilic (pink-staining) material within the glomerular capillary lumina, representing the hyaline thrombus

Look for a delicate fibrin network within the hyaline material, which may be visible as fine strands extending across the capillary lumina. The fibrin network contributes to the stability and structure of the thrombus
Note the degree of luminal occlusion caused by the hyaline thrombus. Thrombi may partially or completely obstruct the capillary lumina, leading to compromised blood flow within the glomerulus
Observe the entrapment of erythrocytes within the hyaline thrombus, contributing to its reddish appearance. Erythrocytes may be seen trapped within the fibrin network
Look for alterations in the glomerular endothelium adjacent to the thrombus, such as endothelial cell activation, swelling, or detachment, which may indicate endothelial injury

Identify signs of associated inflammation, such as infiltrating leukocytes (e.g., neutrophils, monocytes), which may be present in the vicinity of the hyaline thrombus as part of the host response to vascular injury
Observe expansion of the mesangial matrix surrounding the thrombus, which may accompany the inflammatory response and contribute to glomerular injury

Using staining techniques such as periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) or silver stains, observe the hyaline thrombus for characteristic staining patterns, which may help differentiate it from other intraluminal materials
glomerulus_endotheliosis: Identify endothelial cells that appear swollen or enlarged compared to normal. Swelling of the endothelial cells is a characteristic feature of endotheliosis
Note the degree of luminal occlusion caused by the swollen endothelial cells. Endothelial swelling may lead to partial or complete obstruction of the capillary lumina

Look for a double contour appearance of the glomerular basement membrane (GBM), characterized by the presence of an additional layer adjacent to the endothelium. This double contour is a result of endothelial cell protrusions into the GBM
Observe expansion of the mesangial matrix between the capillary loops. Mesangial matrix expansion may accompany endothelial injury and contribute to the thickening of the glomerular tuft

Identify intraluminal fibrin deposits within the capillary lumina, often associated with endothelial injury and activation. Fibrin deposits may appear as eosinophilic material within the capillary loops
Look for loss or attenuation of endothelial fenestrations, which are normally present in glomerular capillaries. Loss of fenestrations is a hallmark of endothelial injury
Determine whether endotheliosis affects the entire glomerulus (global) or only a segment of it (segmental). Segmental involvement may suggest localized injury or disease
Observe for effacement or flattening of podocyte foot processes along the GBM. Podocyte effacement is often associated with endothelial injury and disruption of the glomerular filtration barrier
Look for signs of associated inflammatory infiltrates, such as leukocytes (e.g., neutrophils, monocytes), which may be present in the glomerular tuft or surrounding interstitium
hyalin_drop_diabetic_glomerulus: Identify the presence of eosinophilic (pink-staining) droplets within the glomerular capillary lumina or mesangium. Hyalin droplets typically appear as homogenous, amorphous material
Observe expansion of the mesangial matrix, often accompanied by the deposition of hyalin droplets. Mesangial expansion contributes to the enlargement and distortion of the glomerular tuft
Note the degree of luminal occlusion caused by the hyalin droplets. Luminal occlusion may lead to compromised blood flow within the glomerulus

Consider associated pathological changes characteristic of diabetic glomerulopathy, such as mesangial sclerosis, glomerular basement membrane thickening, and nodular glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules)
Determine whether hyalin droplets are diffusely distributed throughout the glomerulus or present in a segmental pattern. Segmental distribution may indicate focal lesions within the glomerulus
Differentiate hyalin droplets from inflammatory infiltrates by the absence of cellular components within the droplets. Hyalin droplets are primarily composed of proteinaceous material

Using staining techniques such as periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) or trichrome stains, observe the hyalin droplets for characteristic staining patterns. Hyalin material typically stains positive with PAS and appears magenta
Look for alterations in podocyte morphology, including foot process effacement or hypertrophy, which may accompany the presence of hyalin droplets
immature_glomerulus: Note the smaller size and rounder shape of the immature glomerulus compared to mature glomeruli. Immature glomeruli are typically smaller and more globular in appearance.
Identify a less complex and less convoluted capillary tuft structure within the glomerulus. Immature glomeruli may have fewer or less well-defined capillary loops compared to mature glomeruli.
Look for immature podocytes lining the glomerular basement membrane. Immature podocytes may appear less differentiated and exhibit fewer foot processes compared to mature podocytes.
Identify less developed mesangial cells within the mesangium. These cells may appear less abundant and less mature compared to those in mature glomeruli.
Observe a relatively thick glomerular basement membrane (GBM) in immature glomeruli. The GBM may appear thicker compared to that of mature glomeruli due to ongoing development.
Note the absence or underdevelopment of the characteristic capillary loops within the glomerulus. Immature glomeruli may lack the well-defined loops seen in mature glomeruli.

Identify immature blood vessels within the glomerulus, which may have a less organized appearance compared to mature vessels. Immature vessels may lack the distinct arterial and venous components seen in mature glomeruli.

Using staining techniques such as periodic acid-Schiff (PAS), observe the immature glomerulus for characteristic staining patterns. Immature glomeruli may exhibit less intense staining compared to mature glomeruli due to lower cellular and matrix content.
Evaluate the surrounding renal tissue for signs of ongoing nephrogenesis or development, which may support the identification of an immature glomerulus.
ischemic_glomerular_collapse: Identify glomeruli that appear shrunken and collapsed compared to adjacent normal glomeruli. Ischemic glomerular collapse often affects the entire glomerulus uniformly.
Note the reduced size of the collapsed glomerulus, which may appear smaller and more condensed compared to normal glomeruli.
Observe compression or collapse of the glomerular capillary loops within the collapsed glomerulus. Capillary loops may appear flattened or distorted due to decreased blood flow.
Look for thickening of the glomerular basement membrane (GBM) within the collapsed glomerulus. GBM thickening may result from chronic ischemic injury and fibrotic changes.
Identify contraction of the mesangial matrix within the collapsed glomerulus, leading to decreased mesangial cellularity and matrix expansion.
Note adherence of the collapsed glomerulus to Bowman's capsule, which may result from fibrotic adhesions and scarring.
Observe the absence or severe reduction in the number of patent capillary lumina within the collapsed glomerulus. This reflects loss of functional capillary beds and impaired filtration.
Evaluate the surrounding renal tubules and interstitium for signs of chronic ischemic injury, such as tubular atrophy, interstitial fibrosis, and inflammatory cell infiltration.
Look for the presence of foam cells within the collapsed glomerulus, which may indicate lipid accumulation secondary to ischemic injury.
karyorrhexis_glomerulonephritis: Identify pyknotic nuclei within the glomerular tuft or mesangium. Pyknotic nuclei appear condensed, shrunken, and deeply stained compared to normal nuclei.

Look for fragmented nuclei within glomerular cells, such as podocytes, mesangial cells, or endothelial cells. Nuclear fragmentation results in the formation of small, irregularly shaped nuclear remnants.
Identify apoptotic bodies, which are small, round structures containing fragmented nuclear material. Apoptotic bodies may be present within the glomerular tuft or in Bowman's space.
Observe loss of nuclear integrity, characterized by irregular nuclear outlines and fragmentation of chromatin material. This indicates ongoing cellular injury and apoptosis.
Look for signs of associated inflammatory infiltrates, such as leukocytes (e.g., neutrophils, monocytes), which may be present in the glomerular tuft or surrounding interstitium.
Identify increased mesangial cellularity, often accompanied by karyorrhectic nuclei within the mesangium. Mesangial cell hyperplasia is a common feature of proliferative glomerulonephritis.
Assess for changes in endothelial cell morphology, such as endothelial cell activation, swelling, or detachment, which may accompany glomerular inflammation and injury.
Note alterations in capillary loop morphology, including capillary wall thickening, leukocyte infiltration, and luminal occlusion, which may be associated with karyorrhexis.
Using staining techniques such as hematoxylin and eosin (H&E), periodic acid-Schiff (PAS), or silver stains, observe the karyorrhectic nuclei for characteristic staining patterns.
membranous_nephropathy_holes: Identify subepithelial projections or spikes extending into the glomerular basement membrane (GBM) from the underlying podocytes. These spikes represent immune complex deposits and may appear as electron-dense material under electron microscopy

Look for areas of 'holes' or lucent spaces within the GBM, corresponding to regions where the GBM is not covered by subepithelial spikes. These holes are areas of relative GBM thinning and may result from displacement or dissolution of the GBM matrix by immune complex deposition.

Determine whether spikes and holes are diffusely distributed throughout the glomerulus or present in a segmental pattern. Diffuse distribution may suggest widespread immune complex deposition, while segmental distribution may indicate focal lesions.
Thickening of GBM Adjacent to Spikes
Observe thickening of the GBM adjacent to the subepithelial spikes. The thickening may result from the accumulation of immune complexes and associated inflammatory changes.

Look for effacement or flattening of podocyte foot processes along the GBM, which may accompany the formation of subepithelial spikes. Foot process effacement contributes to the disruption of the glomerular filtration barrier.

Using silver stains, such as silver methenamine or silver nitrate, observe the glomerulus for characteristic staining patterns. Subepithelial spikes may appear as black lines or dots, while holes may appear as unstained areas within the GBM.

membranous_nephropathy_spikes: Identify subepithelial projections or spikes extending into the glomerular basement membrane (GBM) from the underlying podocytes. These spikes represent immune complex deposits and may appear as electron-dense material under electron microscopy.
Observe the uniform thickness of the subepithelial spikes along the GBM. Spikes typically have a consistent width and height, contributing to their characteristic appearance.

Determine the distribution pattern of the spikes within the glomerulus. Spikes may be diffusely distributed throughout the GBM or present in a segmental pattern, affecting only certain areas of the glomerulus.
Thickening of GBM Adjacent to Spikes
Look for thickening of the GBM adjacent to the subepithelial spikes. The thickening may result from the accumulation of immune complexes and associated inflammatory changes.

Evaluate podocyte foot processes along the GBM for effacement or flattening. Podocyte foot process effacement contributes to the disruption of the glomerular filtration barrier and is commonly observed in membranous nephropathy.

mesangial_hypercellularity: Identify an increased number of mesangial cells within the mesangium compared to normal. Mesangial hypercellularity is characterized by the presence of numerous mesangial cells filling the mesangial region.
Observe expansion of the mesangial matrix, which may appear widened and more prominent compared to normal. Mesangial hypercellularity is often accompanied by matrix expansion.

Using staining techniques such as periodic acid-Schiff (PAS), observe the mesangial matrix for characteristic staining patterns. Mesangial matrix may stain more intensely due to increased glycoprotein content.

Look for distortion or compression of the glomerular capillary loops resulting from mesangial expansion. Mesangial hypercellularity may lead to compression of capillary lumina and distortion of capillary architecture.
Note the reduced visibility of capillary lumina within the glomerulus due to mesangial expansion and hypercellularity. This may be particularly evident in areas with pronounced mesangial involvement.

Observe compression of glomerular capillaries by expanded mesangial cells and matrix. Mesangial hypercellularity may lead to compression of adjacent endothelial cells and narrowing of capillary lumina.
Evaluate for associated pathological changes, such as mesangial sclerosis, immune complex deposition, or inflammatory infiltrates, which may contribute to mesangial hypercellularity.

Assess the morphology of mesangial cells for evidence of activation or proliferation. Mesangial cells in hypercellular states may appear enlarged, with prominent nuclei and increased cytoplasmic volume.

Using immunofluorescence microscopy, identify characteristic immunofluorescent staining patterns. Mesangial hypercellularity may be associated with increased mesangial staining for immunoglobulins or complement components.
mesangial_matrix_expansion: Identify widening of the mesangial area between the glomerular capillary loops. Mesangial matrix expansion results in increased mesangial volume, leading to a wider mesangial region.

Observe the appearance of the mesangial matrix, which may appear homogeneously eosinophilic (pink-staining) or exhibit granular deposits. These deposits represent accumulated extracellular matrix proteins and glycoproteins.

Using staining techniques such as periodic acid-Schiff (PAS), note the increased intensity of staining within the mesangial matrix. Mesangial matrix expansion may lead to enhanced PAS staining due to increased glycoprotein content.
Look for compression or narrowing of the glomerular capillary loops caused by expanded mesangial matrix. Compression of capillary lumina by the mesangial matrix may distort capillary architecture.
Note the reduced visibility of capillary lumina within the glomerulus due to mesangial matrix expansion. This may be particularly evident in areas with pronounced mesangial involvement.
Assess the staining patterns of the mesangial matrix for characteristic features. Mesangial matrix expansion may exhibit increased intensity and extent of staining compared to normal glomeruli.
Evaluate mesangial cellularity within the mesangium. Mesangial matrix expansion may be accompanied by increased mesangial cellularity or hypertrophy.
Look for associated pathological changes, such as immune complex deposition, mesangial sclerosis, or inflammatory infiltrates, which may contribute to mesangial matrix expansion.

Using immunofluorescence microscopy, identify characteristic immunofluorescent staining patterns. Mesangial matrix expansion may be associated with increased mesangial staining for immunoglobulins or complement components.
mesangiolysis: Thinning or Absence of Mesangial Area

Identify areas within the mesangium where mesangial cells and matrix are thin or absent, resulting in an apparent loss of mesangial structure. Mesangiolysis leads to the disruption of normal mesangial architecture.

Observe irregular or fragmented mesangial areas, where mesangial cells and matrix are discontinuous or fragmented. Mesangiolysis results in the disruption of the meshwork-like structure of the mesangium.

Using staining techniques such as periodic acid-Schiff (PAS), assess the mesangial area for characteristic staining patterns. Areas of mesangiolysis may exhibit decreased PAS staining intensity or complete absence of PAS-positive material.
Look for areas within the mesangium where mesangial cells are sparse or absent. Mesangiolysis involves the loss of mesangial cells, leading to reduced cellularity within affected areas.
Gaps or Spaces Within the Mesangium
Identify gaps or spaces within the mesangium, indicating areas of mesangial cell and matrix loss. These gaps may appear empty or contain cellular debris.
Observe widening of the capillary loops adjacent to areas of mesangiolysis. Disruption of the mesangium may lead to capillary loop dilation or distortion.
Look for signs of glomerular capillary damage, such as endothelial cell detachment or injury, which may accompany mesangiolysis.
Evaluate for associated pathological changes, such as immune complex deposition, glomerular sclerosis, or inflammatory infiltrates, which may contribute to mesangiolysis.

Using immunofluorescence microscopy, identify characteristic immunofluorescent staining patterns. Mesangiolysis may be associated with altered mesangial staining for immunoglobulins or complement components.
nodular_sclerosis_glomerulus: Identify discrete nodular deposits within the glomerular tuft, which may appear as rounded or irregularly shaped eosinophilic (pink-staining) areas. These nodules represent deposits of extracellular matrix proteins, including collagen.
Observe the nodular deposits for a homogeneous appearance under light microscopy. Nodular sclerosis typically presents as homogeneous eosinophilic material without distinct cellular elements.

Determine the distribution pattern of nodular deposits within the glomerulus. Nodular sclerosis may be diffuse, affecting the entire glomerulus, or segmental, involving only a portion of the glomerular tuft.
Note thickening of the glomerular basement membrane (GBM) adjacent to nodular deposits. Nodular sclerosis may lead to GBM thickening due to the accumulation of matrix proteins.
Observe expansion of the mesangial matrix surrounding the nodular deposits. Mesangial matrix expansion may accompany nodular sclerosis and contribute to glomerular tuft distortion.

Look for adhesions between the glomerular tuft and Bowman's capsule, which may be present in areas of nodular sclerosis. Capsular adhesions result from scarring and fibrosis associated with nodular deposits.
Identify compression or narrowing of glomerular capillary lumina adjacent to nodular deposits. Nodular sclerosis may lead to capillary compression and distortion of capillary architecture.

Using silver stains, such as silver methenamine or silver nitrate, observe the glomerulus for characteristic staining patterns. Nodular deposits may appear as black-staining nodules within the glomerular tuft.
Using immunofluorescence microscopy, identify characteristic immunofluorescent staining patterns. Nodular sclerosis may be associated with increased staining for matrix proteins or immunoglobulins.
parietal_cell_glomerulus: Presence of Parietal Epithelial Cells (PECs) on Glomerular Tuft
Identify cells resembling parietal epithelial cells extending from Bowman's capsule onto the glomerular tuft. PECs on the glomerular tuft are characteristic of a parietal cell glomerulus.

Locate PECs on the urinary side of the glomerular basement membrane (GBM) within Bowman's capsule. PECs should be distinguished from podocytes, which are normally located on the vascular side of the GBM.
Differentiate PECs from podocytes based on their morphology. PECs typically have a squamous or cuboidal appearance, in contrast to the characteristic arborized shape of podocytes.
Look for an increased number of PECs within Bowman's capsule, indicating parietal cell hyperplasia. Parietal cell hyperplasia may be observed in response to glomerular injury or inflammation.

Note any loss of podocytes from the glomerular tuft, which may accompany the presence of PECs on the glomerular tuft. Podocyte loss is a common feature of glomerular diseases associated with parietal cell glomeruli.

Identify tubular extensions originating from Bowman's capsule, which may be present in association with parietal cell glomeruli. These tubular extensions represent an aberrant anatomical arrangement and may extend into the urinary space.
Evaluate for associated pathological changes, such as glomerular sclerosis, mesangial proliferation, or inflammatory infiltrates, which may accompany parietal cell glomeruli.

Using silver stains, such as silver methenamine or silver nitrate, observe the glomerulus for characteristic staining patterns. Parietal cell glomeruli may exhibit altered staining patterns compared to normal glomeruli.

Using immunofluorescence microscopy, identify characteristic immunofluorescent staining patterns. Parietal cell glomeruli may be associated with increased staining for markers of inflammation or injury.
periglomerular_fibrosis: Identify areas of increased collagen deposition surrounding the glomerulus. Periglomerular fibrosis manifests as the accumulation of collagen fibers in the interstitium adjacent to the glomerulus.
Observe widening of the interstitial space surrounding the glomerulus. Periglomerular fibrosis results in the expansion of the interstitial compartment due to the deposition of fibrotic tissue.
Look for fibrotic bands or tracts extending from the glomerulus into the adjacent interstitium. These bands represent areas of collagen accumulation and fibrotic remodeling.
Note distortion or compression of renal tubules adjacent to fibrotic areas. Periglomerular fibrosis may lead to compression of tubular structures, affecting their morphology.
Identify disruption or loss of normal tissue architecture in the periglomerular region. Fibrotic changes result in the replacement of functional tissue with fibrous scar tissue.

Using staining techniques such as Masson's trichrome or Sirius Red, observe the periglomerular area for characteristic staining patterns. Collagen fibers typically stain blue or red, highlighting areas of fibrosis.
Evaluate for associated glomerular pathologies, such as glomerulosclerosis or glomerulonephritis, which may precede or coincide with periglomerular fibrosis.
Look for inflammatory cell infiltrates within the periglomerular fibrotic areas, which may indicate ongoing inflammation and tissue remodeling.
Assess the extent and severity of periglomerular fibrosis, ranging from focal to diffuse involvement around the glomerulus.
podocyte: Location Along the Glomerular Basement Membrane (GBM)
Identify cells lining the outer aspect of the glomerular capillaries, adhering to the GBM. Podocytes are located on the visceral layer of Bowman's capsule, covering the capillary loops.

Observe the arborized or 'foot-like' extensions of podocytes, known as foot processes or pedicels, which interdigitate to form filtration slits. These foot processes contribute to the filtration barrier of the glomerulus.

Look for flattened or irregularly shaped cells with multiple processes extending from the cell body. Podocytes typically have a unique morphology characterized by a cell body with numerous extensions.

Note the position of the podocyte nucleus, which is often located centrally within the cell body. The presence of a centrally located nucleus distinguishes podocytes from mesangial cells and parietal epithelial cells.

Using electron microscopy, identify the presence of slit diaphragms or gap junctions between adjacent foot processes of podocytes. These structures contribute to the selective permeability of the glomerular filtration barrier.

Using staining techniques such as periodic acid-Schiff (PAS), observe the glomerulus for characteristic staining patterns of podocytes. Podocytes may stain lightly with PAS due to their low cytoplasmic content.

Employ immunohistochemical staining for podocyte-specific markers, such as podocin, synaptopodin, WT1 (Wilms tumor 1), or nephrin. Positive staining for these markers confirms the presence of podocytes.
Confirm the association of podocytes with glomerular capillaries, forming the visceral layer of Bowman's capsule and enveloping the capillary loops.

Assess the size and density of podocytes within the glomerulus. Podocytes are relatively large cells compared to endothelial cells and mesangial cells, and they cover the entire surface of the capillary loops.
podocyte_hyperplasia: Identify areas within the glomerulus where the density of podocytes is higher than normal. Podocyte hyperplasia results in an increased number of podocytes per glomerular tuft.
Observe crowding of podocyte cell bodies within Bowman's capsule and along the glomerular capillaries. Increased podocyte density may lead to overlapping or crowding of podocyte cell bodies.
Note enlargement of the glomerular tuft due to the presence of additional podocytes. Podocyte hyperplasia may result in expansion of the glomerular tuft to accommodate the increased number of cells.
Assess the morphology of podocytes for evidence of hyperplasia. Podocytes may appear enlarged or hypertrophied compared to normal, with prominent nuclei and increased cytoplasmic volume.

Using staining techniques such as periodic acid-Schiff (PAS), observe the glomerulus for characteristic staining patterns of podocytes. Podocyte hyperplasia may result in increased PAS staining intensity or a larger area of PAS-positive staining.
Look for nuclear crowding within Bowman's capsule and along the glomerular tuft, indicating an increased number of podocyte nuclei in these areas.

Using electron microscopy, identify an increased number of podocyte foot processes covering the glomerular basement membrane (GBM). Podocyte hyperplasia may lead to the proliferation of foot processes to accommodate the enlarged glomerular tuft.

Employ immunohistochemical staining for podocyte-specific markers, such as podocin, synaptopodin, or WT1 (Wilms tumor 1). Increased expression of these markers confirms the presence of hyperplastic podocytes.
Evaluate for associated glomerular pathologies, such as glomerulonephritis or diabetic nephropathy, which may precede or coincide with podocyte hyperplasia.
podocyte_hypertrophy: Identify podocyte cell bodies that appear larger or more prominent than normal within Bowman's capsule and along the glomerular capillaries. Enlarged podocyte cell bodies are indicative of hypertrophy.
Observe an increased volume of cytoplasm within hypertrophied podocytes compared to normal. Podocyte hypertrophy leads to an expansion of cytoplasmic content within the cell body.
Assess the morphology of podocytes for evidence of hypertrophy. Hypertrophied podocytes may appear swollen or distended, with enlarged nuclei and increased cytoplasmic granules.
Look for enlargement or hypertrophy of podocyte nuclei within Bowman's capsule and along the glomerular tuft. Hypertrophied podocytes often exhibit enlarged nuclei compared to normal.

Using staining techniques such as periodic acid-Schiff (PAS), observe the glomerulus for characteristic staining patterns of podocytes. Hypertrophied podocytes may exhibit increased PAS staining intensity or a larger area of PAS-positive staining.

Using electron microscopy, identify alterations in podocyte foot processes, such as hypertrophy or effacement. Podocyte hypertrophy may lead to the enlargement or broadening of foot processes covering the glomerular basement membrane (GBM).

Employ immunohistochemical staining for podocyte-specific markers, such as podocin, synaptopodin, or WT1 (Wilms tumor 1). Increased expression of these markers confirms the presence of hypertrophic podocytes.
Evaluate for associated glomerular pathologies, such as glomerulonephritis or diabetic nephropathy, which may precede or coincide with podocyte hypertrophy.
podocyte_reabsorption_droplet: Identify vacuoles or droplets within the cytoplasm of podocytes. These intracellular structures appear as clear or pale-staining rounded or oval bodies.
Observe variability in the size and shape of reabsorption droplets within podocytes. Droplets may range from small, discrete vacuoles to larger, more prominent structures.
Look for vacuoles or droplets within the nucleus of podocytes. In some cases, reabsorption droplets may be present within the podocyte nucleus, contributing to its enlargement.

Using staining techniques such as periodic acid-Schiff (PAS), observe the glomerulus for characteristic staining patterns of reabsorption droplets. Podocyte reabsorption droplets typically stain lightly with PAS, appearing pale or clear.

Utilize special staining techniques such as Oil Red O to visualize lipid droplets within podocytes. Lipid droplets stain red with Oil Red O, facilitating their identification within podocyte cytoplasm.
Confirm the presence of reabsorption droplets within the cytoplasm of podocytes, typically located near the cell periphery or adjacent to the cell nucleus.
Evaluate for associated clinical findings, such as proteinuria or nephrotic syndrome, which may suggest a proteinuric condition predisposing to the formation of reabsorption droplets.
Assess for evidence of podocyte hypertrophy or injury, as reabsorption droplets may be associated with podocyte dysfunction and structural changes.

Using electron microscopy, confirm the presence of lipid droplets within podocytes at the ultrastructural level. Electron microscopy allows for the visualization of intracellular lipid droplets with high resolution.
pseudocrescent: Identify areas within Bowman's space that appear cellular or contain material resembling a crescent. However, upon closer inspection, pseudocrescents lack the cellular infiltrates typically seen in true cellular crescents.

Evaluate the cellular composition of the structure. Pseudocrescents may contain cells such as macrophages, foam cells, or degenerated podocytes but lack the characteristic arrangement and organization seen in cellular crescents.

Assess the organization and alignment of cells within the structure. Pseudocrescents often lack the cohesive arrangement of cells observed in true crescents, with cells appearing more randomly distributed.
Look for the presence of foam cells within the structure. Foam cells, which are lipid-laden macrophages, may be present in pseudocrescents and contribute to their appearance.
Confirm the location of the structure within Bowman's space. Pseudocrescents typically adhere to the Bowman's capsule or extend into Bowman's space without invading the glomerular tuft.

Using staining techniques such as periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) or trichrome stains, observe the structure for characteristic staining patterns. Pseudocrescents may stain differently from true crescents due to differences in cellular composition.
Evaluate for associated glomerular pathologies, such as focal segmental glomerulosclerosis or diabetic nephropathy, which may predispose to the formation of pseudocrescents.
Assess for evidence of podocyte injury or loss, which may contribute to the formation of pseudocrescents in certain glomerular diseases.
solidified_glomerular_sclerosis_global: Identify areas within the glomerulus where the normal glomerular architecture is entirely replaced by fibrous tissue. There should be no remaining capillary loops or recognizable glomerular structures.

Observe a homogeneous appearance of the sclerotic area, which lacks the variability in staining and structure typically seen in normal glomeruli. Fibrous tissue appears uniformly dense and eosinophilic.
Confirm the absence of capillary loops within the glomerulus. Solidified global sclerosis is characterized by the complete obliteration of capillary loops, leaving behind only fibrous tissue.

Look for abundant collagen deposition within the sclerotic area. Collagen fibers replace the normal glomerular components and contribute to the dense, fibrotic appearance of solidified global sclerosis.
Note adhesions between the glomerular tuft and Bowman's capsule. Solidified global sclerosis often results in adhesions that tether the fibrous tissue to the surrounding capsule.

Be aware of potential shrinkage artifact, which may lead to apparent glomerular collapse. However, solidified global sclerosis should be distinguished from glomerular collapse by the absence of residual capillary loops.

Using staining techniques such as periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) or trichrome stains, observe the sclerotic area for characteristic staining patterns. Fibrous tissue typically stains intensely with PAS and may appear blue with trichrome stains.
Assess the extent of sclerosis within the glomerulus. Solidified global sclerosis typically involves the entire glomerular tuft rather than being focal or segmental.

If available, confirm the absence of residual capillary loops and the presence of fibrous tissue by electron microscopy. Electron microscopy provides high-resolution images that can further characterize the fibrotic changes in solidified global sclerosis.
spikes_glomerular_amyoidosis: Identify areas within the glomerulus where there is extracellular deposition of amorphous, eosinophilic material. Amyloid deposits may appear as pale, homogeneous material within the glomerular tuft.

Examine the tissue under polarized light microscopy to visualize the characteristic birefringent 'spikes' or 'stains' produced by amyloid fibrils. Amyloid fibrils exhibit apple-green birefringence when viewed under polarized light.
Note the fine, filamentous appearance of amyloid fibrils within the glomerulus. Amyloid fibrils may appear as delicate strands or fibers interspersed within the glomerular matrix.

Assess the distribution of amyloid deposits within the glomerulus. In spikes glomerular amyloidosis, amyloid deposits are typically widespread throughout the glomerular tuft, giving rise to the appearance of spikes when viewed under polarized light.

Look for involvement of the mesangial matrix by amyloid deposits. Spikes glomerular amyloidosis often results in diffuse deposition of amyloid within the mesangium, contributing to the appearance of spikes.
Observe for thickening of the glomerular basement membrane (GBM) in areas of amyloid deposition. Amyloid fibrils may accumulate within the GBM, leading to its thickening and distortion.

Utilize Congo Red staining to confirm the presence of amyloid deposits within the glomerulus. Amyloid deposits typically stain pink with Congo Red but do not exhibit apple-green birefringence until viewed under polarized light.

Employ immunohistochemical staining for amyloid-specific markers, such as anti-amyloid antibodies or serum amyloid P component (SAP). Positive immunostaining for amyloid markers confirms the presence of amyloid deposits within the glomerulus.
visceral_epithelial_cell: Identify cells located on the visceral layer of Bowman's capsule, covering the outer surface of the glomerular capillaries. Podocytes form the outermost layer of Bowman's capsule and envelop the capillary loops.

Observe the characteristic morphology of podocytes, which includes a cell body with multiple processes or extensions known as foot processes. Podocytes often appear flattened and irregularly shaped, with cytoplasmic extensions extending from the cell body.

Look for foot processes extending from the cell body of podocytes. These foot processes interdigitate with neighboring podocytes and form filtration slits, contributing to the selective permeability of the glomerular filtration barrier.

Note the position of the podocyte nucleus within the cell body. In podocytes, the nucleus is typically located centrally within the cell, distinguishing them from other cell types within the glomerulus.
Assess the density of cytoplasm within podocytes. Podocytes often have relatively sparse cytoplasm compared to other cell types within the glomerulus.

Confirm the association of podocytes with glomerular capillaries. Podocytes wrap around the capillary loops, forming a physical barrier between the blood within the capillaries and the urinary space within Bowman's capsule.

Utilize immunohistochemical staining for podocyte-specific markers, such as podocin, synaptopodin, WT1 (Wilms tumor 1), or nephrin. Positive staining for these markers confirms the presence of podocytes.

Consider ultrastructural features observed using electron microscopy, such as the presence of slit diaphragms or gap junctions between adjacent foot processes. These ultrastructural features are characteristic of podocytes and contribute to their function in maintaining the glomerular filtration barrier.
visceral_epithelial_cell_capping: Identify areas within the glomerulus where podocytes appear to aggregate or accumulate at the top of the glomerular tuft, resembling a cap-like structure.
Observe a concentration of podocyte cell bodies at the top of the glomerular tuft, forming a layer that extends beyond the normal distribution of podocytes.

Assess the morphology of podocytes forming the cap. These podocytes may exhibit altered morphology compared to podocytes in the rest of the glomerulus, with irregular cell shapes and prominent cytoplasmic extensions.

Confirm the location of the podocyte cap relative to Bowman's capsule and the glomerular tuft. Podocytes forming the cap should be observed on the visceral side of Bowman's capsule, extending over the glomerular tuft.
Note the disruption of normal glomerular architecture caused by the podocyte cap. The cap may obscure the underlying capillary loops and alter the distribution of other glomerular cell types.
Evaluate for associated glomerular pathologies, such as focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) or membranous nephropathy, which are commonly associated with visceral epithelial cell capping.

Using staining techniques such as periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) or trichrome stains, observe the podocyte cap for characteristic staining patterns. Podocytes forming the cap may exhibit altered staining patterns compared to normal podocytes.

Employ immunohistochemical staining for podocyte-specific markers, such as podocin, synaptopodin, or WT1 (Wilms tumor 1). Altered expression of these markers in podocytes forming the cap may be observed.
wire_loop_glomerulus: Identify areas within the glomerulus where the capillary loops appear thickened, hyalinized, and eosinophilic. These loops may exhibit a concentric or homogenous appearance, resembling loops of wire.
Observe a uniform thickening of the capillary walls throughout the glomerulus. The thickening may involve both the endothelial and mesangial components of the capillary walls.

Note the disruption of normal capillary architecture caused by the thickened and hyalinized loops. The loops may appear rigid and distorted, leading to the loss of the typical delicate appearance of capillary loops.

Evaluate for associated glomerular pathologies, particularly lupus nephritis, where wire loop lesions are commonly observed. Other conditions associated with wire loop appearance include immune complex-mediated glomerulonephritis.

Using staining techniques such as periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) or trichrome stains, observe the capillary loops for characteristic staining patterns. Thickened and hyalinized capillary loops may stain intensely with PAS and exhibit a bluish hue with trichrome stains.

Assess immunofluorescence findings if available, as wire loop lesions in lupus nephritis typically show deposits of immune complexes, particularly IgG and complement components, along the capillary walls.

Look for the presence of subendothelial deposits along the capillary walls, which may contribute to the thickening and hyalinization of the loops. These deposits can be visualized using electron microscopy.
